explanations.explanation: That's the word. Verse 1 says, "…he who hates correction is stupid." It's blunt, and it sits right next to the person who loves discipline and so loves knowledge. Correction stings for a second, but a cookie that never gets corrected comes out of the oven looking like a hockey puck.

Lazy does show up in this chapter, but it comes later, in verse 24: "laziness ends in forced labor." Verse 1 uses a different word for the one who hates correction. It says he "is stupid." You grabbed a word from the right neighborhood, friend, just a different house.

I get why proud came to mind, since hating correction can feel like pride. But the verse doesn't use that word. It says the one who hates correction "is stupid." The text gives us the word and leaves it there, so I'll leave it there too.

Yes, verse 3 says, "…the righteous cannot be uprooted." A man can't be established through wickedness, but the righteous stay put. Picture a tree that no wind can pull out of the ground. Verse 12 comes back to roots, too, saying the root of the righteous flourishes.

I see why that sounds comforting. But the verse never says anything about being forgotten. It says the righteous "cannot be uprooted." Stick with what the text says, friend, because it's already good news.

Deceit is all over this chapter, so that guess makes sense. But verse 3 isn't about being deceived. It says a man can't be established through wickedness, but "the righteous cannot be uprooted." That's the word the verse picks.

That's it. Verse 4 says, "A wife of noble character is her husband's crown…" A crown is something you wear on your head for everyone to see. I'd say that's about as high a compliment as a proverb can give.
A shield is a strong picture, and I can see why it came to mind. But verse 4 doesn't use it. It says a wife of noble character is "her husband's crown." Crown, not shield, friend.
A lamp is a nice picture, but that's not the one in this verse. Verse 4 says a wife of noble character is "her husband's crown." The lamp can stay on the shelf for this one.

Right, verse 6 says, "…the speech of the upright rescues them." Look at the two sides of it. The words of the wicked "lie in wait for blood," and the words of the upright do the opposite. Same mouth equipment, totally different results.

Traps does show up in this chapter, but in verse 13, where an evil man "is trapped by his rebellious speech." Verse 6 is a different line. There, the speech of the upright "rescues them." It's a nice mix-up, friend, because both verses are about words.

Shame shows up in verse 4, with the wife who causes it. In verse 6, though, the upright aren't shamed at all. The speech of the upright "rescues them." The wicked are the ones with the dangerous words here.

I think the first half pulled you along, and I don't blame you. The wicked are overthrown and perish, yes. But the verse turns right there: "…but the house of the righteous will stand." The two houses don't end up in the same place.
That's right, it's false. Verse 7 says, "The wicked are overthrown and perish, but the house of the righteous will stand." Notice that little word "but." It's where the verse swings the other way.

Yes. Verse 8 says, "A man is praised according to his wisdom…" The other side of it is that "a twisted mind is despised." The proverb isn't asking what's in your wallet. It's asking what's in your head.
I get it, people do notice money. But verse 8 doesn't list wealth. It says a man is praised "according to his wisdom." The verse leaves the bank account out of it.
Family matters a lot, and this chapter even talks about a husband and wife. But verse 8 says a man is praised "according to his wisdom." Family isn't the measure in this one.

Correct. Verse 9 says, "Better to be lightly esteemed yet have a servant, than to be self-important but lack food." The self-important man has the big attitude and the empty table. I'll take the full table, friend, and let the attitude go.
Friends would be a sad thing to lack, but that's not what verse 9 says. It says, "…than to be self-important but lack food." The empty thing here is the table, not the guest list.

Land does come up soon, in verse 11, where a man works his land. In verse 9, though, the self-important man lacks something else. The verse says he lacks "food." Hold onto that land for the next verse.

Yes, verse 10 says, "…the tender mercies of the wicked are only cruelty." The wicked might call it mercy, but the verse says that's all it ever is: cruelty. The righteous man, meanwhile, regards the life of his animal.
I can see how "tender mercies" sounds like kindness. That's the trick of the verse. It says the tender mercies of the wicked are "only cruelty." So what looks soft is not soft at all.
Weakness is a clever guess, but the verse doesn't go there. It says the tender mercies of the wicked are "only cruelty." The contrast is with the righteous man who regards the life of his animal.

That's right. Verse 11 says, "The one who works his land will have plenty of food, but whoever chases fantasies lacks judgment." One man is out in the field. The other is out chasing something that isn't there. I think the field man goes home with the better dinner.
Borrowing is a fair thing to wonder about, but verse 11 doesn't mention it. The one who lacks judgment is "whoever chases fantasies." The text puts it right against the one who works his land.

Verse 11 never says anything about hiring workers. It says the man who works his land has plenty of food, but "whoever chases fantasies lacks judgment." The contrast is between real work and chasing what isn't real.

True. Verse 13 says, "An evil man is trapped by his rebellious speech, but a righteous man escapes from trouble." His own mouth sets the trap for the evil man. The righteous man walks out of trouble instead.

I think the first half made this one feel too good to be true. But it is true. Verse 13 says, "An evil man is trapped by his rebellious speech, but a righteous man escapes from trouble." The righteous man does get out.

That's it. Verse 14 says, "By fruitful speech a man is filled with good things, and the work of his hands returns to him." Words and work both come back around. Mine only come back around when I say something to the cookie boxes.

Giving is a good thing, and it's easy to see why you picked it. But verse 14 doesn't say it. It says, "By fruitful speech a man is filled with good things…" The verse is about what comes out of the mouth.
Planning shows up in verse 5, but verse 14 is a different line. It says, "By fruitful speech a man is filled with good things…" The word is speech, friend, so it's about what we say.
Yes. Verse 15 says, "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to counsel." The fool is sure he's right. The wise man is willing to hear someone else out.
That one's pretty close to the fool's side of the verse. The fool's way "is right in his own eyes." The wise man, by contrast, "listens to counsel." So the wise one lets someone else speak up.
Following a crowd isn't what verse 15 says. It says a wise man "listens to counsel." That's listening to advice, which is a different thing from going wherever everyone else is going.

Right. Verse 16 says, "A fool's anger is known at once, but a prudent man overlooks an insult." The prudent man lets it slide. I've been called a lot of names in my day, and letting some of them go sure beats carrying them around.
Handing an insult right back is easy, and I get why you picked it. But verse 16 puts that on the fool's side, where anger "is known at once." The prudent man "overlooks an insult."
Reporting it makes sense if you're picturing a modern workplace. But verse 16 says nothing about that. The prudent man "overlooks an insult." He lets it pass.
Yes. Verse 18 says, "Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing." Same tongue, two very different results. One cuts and the other mends.
Silence can be wise, and verse 23 touches on keeping knowledge to yourself. But verse 18 says something else. The tongue of the wise "brings healing." It's the speaking that heals here.
Riches would be a nice reward, but verse 18 doesn't promise them. It says, "…the tongue of the wise brings healing." Healing is the word, friend.
True. Verse 19 says, "Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment." Forever on one side and a moment on the other. That's not even a close race.
I think "only a moment" sounded too short to be true. But it is true. Verse 19 says, "Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment." Honest words last and lies don't.

That's it. Verse 20 says, "Deceit is in the hearts of those who devise evil, but the counselors of peace have joy." Deceit sits in one set of hearts and joy sits in the other. I'd pick the joy every time.
Power might sound like the thing counselors want. But verse 20 doesn't say it. The counselors of peace "have joy."
Fame is a fun guess, but it isn't in this verse. Verse 20 says the counselors of peace "have joy." No spotlight needed.

I can see why the second half might sound plausible. But the verse says the opposite. Verse 21 says, "No harm befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble." The righteous side gets no harm, and the wicked side gets trouble.
Yes, it's false. Verse 21 says, "No harm befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble." The trouble goes to the wicked, and the righteous get no harm.
That's right. Verse 22 says, "Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight." Think about what that means. The faithful ones bring Him delight.
Boldness can be a good thing, but verse 22 doesn't name it. It says, "…those who deal faithfully are His delight." The word is faithfully, friend.
Rising early sounds responsible, and I respect it, even if my alarm and I don't always agree. But verse 22 says something else. It says, "…those who deal faithfully are His delight."
Yes. Verse 24 says, "The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor." The diligent hand rules, and the lazy one ends up working under somebody else. That's a rough swap.
Clever is a good quality, and I see why it came to mind. But verse 24 says, "The hand of the diligent will rule…" It's the hard worker the verse puts first.
Might sounds like a ruler's word. But verse 24 isn't talking about strength. It says, "The hand of the diligent will rule…" The one who keeps working is the one in view.

Right. Verse 25 says, "Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up." It doesn't take a speech. One good word does it. I've seen a kind word do more for a worn-out stamper than a whole box of fresh dough.
Rest feels like it should be the answer, and a nap never hurt anybody. But verse 25 says, "…a good word cheers it up." The cheer comes from what someone says.
A full purse might help with some worries, I'll give you that. But verse 25 doesn't mention it. It says, "…a good word cheers it up."
True. Verse 26 says, "A righteous man is cautious in friendship, but the ways of the wicked lead them astray." The righteous man is careful. The wicked go astray.

I think "cautious" might have sounded strange for a righteous man. But it's right there in verse 26: "A righteous man is cautious in friendship…" The other half says the ways of the wicked lead them astray.
Yes. Verse 28 says, "There is life in the path of righteousness, but another path leads to death." Two paths, and the proverbs close on that note. The chapter ends by pointing to life.
Honor is a good guess, and verse 8 does talk about being praised. But verse 28 is the closing line, and it says, "There is life in the path of righteousness…" The word is life.
Strength sounds like a fair reward for staying on a path. But verse 28 says, "There is life in the path of righteousness, but another path leads to death." Life is what it names, friend.
